name: ltrace
one_line: trace the library calls of a program
plain: `ltrace` shows each call a program makes into shared libraries (strcmp, strlen, malloc, printf, puts, memcmp...) with the arguments and the return values. For a simple crackme that calls strcmp(your_input, secret), ltrace prints both strings, giving you the secret straight away.
It is the quick first step before opening a disassembler. It only sees dynamic library calls, so statically linked or stripped-down programs may show little; use strace or gdb then.
when: Reveal what a crackme compares your input with.

examples.title: Trace a program
examples.explain: Each line is a call like strcmp("guess", "s3cret") = -1. Run it with a wrong answer and read both arguments.

examples.title: Show system calls too
examples.explain: -S also prints system calls (like strace). Noisy but complete.

examples.title: Longer strings
examples.explain: -s sets the maximum string length shown (default 32).

examples.title: Count and summarise
examples.explain: -c prints a table of calls and time spent.

mistakes: Expecting a result on a static or Go/Rust binary: little or no library calls appear.
Reading only the first strcmp: your input may be compared to several strings.
Forgetting that the real secret may be transformed first (XOR, base64) before it is compared.
Running an unknown binary outside a VM: ltrace runs it for real.
Not trying strace when ltrace shows nothing.
